subject: Physics
title: Current Electricity
summary: Current is the rate of flow of charge, I = dq/dt. Electrons in a conductor move randomly; an applied field gives them a small average drift velocity (~10⁻⁴ m/s) — I = neAv_d. A bulb lights at once because the field spreads through the wire at nearly the speed of light.
Ohm's law V = IR (at constant temperature). Resistance depends on material (ρ), length and area: R = ρl/A. Resistance of metals rises with temperature; that of semiconductors falls.

A real cell has emf E and internal resistance r: terminal voltage V = E − Ir (discharging). Resistances add in series and their reciprocals add in parallel. Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; maximum power is delivered when the load R = r.

Kirchhoff's two rules (junction: ΣI = 0 — charge conservation; loop: ΣV = 0 — energy conservation) solve any circuit. A Wheatstone bridge balances when P/Q = R/S; the meter bridge uses this to measure an unknown resistance.

formulas.name: Electric current
formulas.formula: I = dq/dt;   average I = Δq/Δt;   1 A = 1 C/s
formulas.note: Current is a scalar — although it has a direction, it doesn't add like a vector.

formulas.name: Drift velocity and mobility
formulas.formula: I = neAv_d;   v_d = eEτ/m;   mobility μ = v_d/E = eτ/m
formulas.note: v_d is tiny (~mm/s); the thermal speed of electrons (~10⁵ m/s) is a different thing.

formulas.name: Current density and microscopic Ohm's law
formulas.formula: J = I/A = nev_d;   J = σE;   σ = 1/ρ = ne²τ/m
formulas.when: Local relation between field and current.
formulas.note: J is a vector, I a scalar.

formulas.name: Ohm's law and resistance
formulas.formula: V = IR;   R = ρl/A;   unit ohm (Ω)
formulas.note: Ohm's law doesn't hold for all devices — diodes and thermistors are non-ohmic.

formulas.name: Stretching a wire
formulas.formula: Same volume: l → nl ⇒ R → n²R;   radius → r/n ⇒ R → n⁴R
formulas.mistake: Doubling the length also halves the area — so 4 times, not 2 times.

formulas.name: Temperature dependence
formulas.formula: ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)];   R_T = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]
formulas.note: α is positive for metals, negative for semiconductors, very small for alloys (manganin, constantan).

formulas.name: Colour code
formulas.formula: B B R O Y G B V G W = 0–9 (Black Brown Red Orange Yellow Green Blue Violet Grey White);  first two bands digits, third multiplier (10ⁿ), fourth tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%, none 20%)

formulas.name: Series and parallel resistors
formulas.formula: Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … (same I);   parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same V)
formulas.note: The parallel equivalent is smaller than the smallest resistor.

formulas.name: EMF, internal resistance, terminal voltage
formulas.formula: I = E/(R + r);   discharging V = E − Ir;   charging V = E + Ir;   open circuit V = E
formulas.note: Terminal voltage exceeds the emf only while charging.

formulas.name: Cells in series and parallel
formulas.formula: n in series: E_eq = nE, r_eq = nr;   m in parallel (identical): E_eq = E, r_eq = r/m;   mixed: I = nE/(R + nr/m)
formulas.mistake: A cell connected the wrong way reduces the emf, but its r still adds.

formulas.name: Electric power and energy
formulas.formula: P = VI = I²R = V²/R;   energy = Pt;   1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
formulas.note: In series (same I) the larger R glows more; in parallel (same V) the smaller R glows more.

formulas.name: Maximum power transfer
formulas.note: At maximum power the efficiency is only 50%.

formulas.name: Kirchhoff's rules
formulas.formula: Junction: ΣI_in = ΣI_out (charge conservation);   loop: ΣΔV = 0 (energy conservation)
formulas.note: In a loop, going through a battery from − to + counts +E; through a resistor along the current counts −IR.

formulas.name: Wheatstone bridge
formulas.formula: Balanced: P/Q = R/S ⇒ no current in the galvanometer
formulas.note: At balance remove the galvanometer branch — the circuit becomes simple.

formulas.name: Meter bridge
formulas.formula: X/R = l/(100 − l)   (l in cm, on the side of unknown X)
formulas.note: Errors are smallest with the balance point near the middle (end correction).

examples.title: Drift velocity
examples.problem: A copper wire of area 1 mm² carries 1.5 A, n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. v_d?

examples.title: Stretched wire
examples.problem: A 10 Ω wire is stretched to double its length (same volume). New R?

examples.title: Network
examples.problem: 2, 3 and 6 Ω in parallel, then 4 Ω in series; 10 V battery. Total R and current?

examples.title: Real cell
examples.problem: E = 12 V, r = 0.5 Ω, R = 5.5 Ω. Current and terminal voltage?

examples.title: Maximum power
examples.problem: E = 12 V, r = 2 Ω. Maximum power to the load?

examples.title: Cells in series
examples.problem: 4 cells (1.5 V, 0.5 Ω each) in series with R = 4 Ω. Current?

examples.title: Kirchhoff: two batteries
examples.problem: A 6 V cell (branch resistance 2 Ω) and a 3 V cell (branch 1 Ω) in parallel both feed a 2 Ω load. Load and branch currents?
examples.solution: Top-node voltage V: (6 − V)/2 + (3 − V)/1 = V/2 ⇒ V = 3 V. Load = 1.5 A; 6 V branch = 1.5 A; 3 V branch = 0 A (the 3 V cell is neither charging nor discharging).

examples.title: Meter bridge
examples.problem: 30 Ω in the right gap; balance at 40 cm from the left end. Unknown X?

examples.title: Bulb at half voltage
examples.problem: A 100 W, 220 V bulb runs on 110 V. R and power?
examples.solution: R = V²/P = 484 Ω. P = 110²/484 = 25 W (one quarter).

examples.title: Colour code
examples.problem: Bands brown, black, red, gold. Resistance?

topics.title: Electric current and drift
topics.explain: Free electrons in a wire move randomly at ~10⁵ m/s with zero net flow. An applied field gives them a drift. The relaxation time τ is the average time between collisions; it falls as temperature rises, so ρ of a metal increases.

topics.title: Ohmic and non-ohmic devices
topics.explain: Ohmic: V–I graph a straight line through the origin (metals at constant T). Non-ohmic: diodes (one direction), thermistors, GaAs (negative resistance region), electrolytes.

topics.title: Comparing resistivities
topics.explain: Metals ~10⁻⁸ Ω·m, semiconductors in between, insulators above ~10¹⁴ Ω·m. Nichrome for heater elements (high ρ, high melting point); manganin/constantan for standard resistors (very small α); copper for connecting wires (low ρ).

topics.title: Cells: emf and terminal voltage
topics.explain: Emf is the energy a cell gives per unit charge, not a potential difference across a resistor. Drawing current causes a voltage drop across the internal resistance. An old battery has a larger r.

topics.title: Solving with Kirchhoff's rules
topics.explain: Assume a current in each branch (a wrong direction just gives a negative answer). Apply the junction rule at independent junctions and the loop rule around independent loops, then solve. In symmetric circuits join or split points at equal potential to simplify.

topics.title: Wheatstone bridge and meter bridge
topics.explain: At balance both ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential. In a meter bridge a jockey slides along a 1 m uniform wire (manganin/constantan) to find balance. Sensitivity is highest when all four resistances are nearly equal.

topics.title: Heating effect
topics.explain: Joule heating H = I²Rt. A fuse wire has a low melting point and high resistance — it melts at large current and breaks the circuit. Power is transmitted at high voltage so that I²R loss is small.
